questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A written accent on a word whose last syllable is stressed
questions.learningObjective: decide from the ending and the position of the stress whether a word takes a written accent
questions.stem: Spanish marks stress in writing, and three endings call for a written accent: a vowel, n and s. A menu in a Spanish coffee bar lists 'un café con leche', 'un té' and 'un chocolate'. Which statement about those three words is correct?

options.text: All three need an accent, since a word ending in a vowel is always stressed on that last syllable
options.misconception: assumes a final vowel always carries the stress and so always needs marking

options.text: Cafe must carry the accent, because its last syllable is stressed and it ends in a vowel
None of the three needs an accent, since a word ending in a vowel is easy to stress without marking it
options.misconception: treats a final vowel as a standing exemption from the accent rule

options.text: Only cafe needs the accent, and the reason is its number of syllables rather than its stress
options.misconception: bases the accent on a syllable count instead of on which syllable is stressed

questions.explanation: The test has three steps and no fourth: count the syllables, look at the ending, and place the accent on the stressed syllable. Cafe is ca-fe, so the last syllable is stressed and the word ends in a vowel, which is one of the three endings that oblige a written accent. The same reasoning would give the first word of cafe con leche the same mark, and would leave chocolate unmarked, since it is cho-co-la-te with the stress on the penult and a final vowel. The trap in the other options is stopping after the first two steps, in one direction or the other, and treating the ending as the decision rather than as one of three inputs.
questions.hint: Count the syllables, then ask which of them is the stressed one.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Counting a diphthong as one syllable in the accent test
questions.learningObjective: count a diphthong as a single syllable before applying the accent rules
questions.stem: Two everyday Spanish words both contain the letters a and u. One is written 'causa' and the other 'baúl'. A learner claims the two must be stressed the same way because the vowel pair is the same. What settles the difference?

options.text: Both words keep the pair as one diphthong, so both are two syllables and the accent rule that applies to each is the same rule
options.misconception: assumes the letter pair settles the syllable count on its own, whatever the stress does to it

options.text: Only the first keeps the pair as one diphthong, while in the second the u is stressed and closed, so the two vowels are in hiatus and a mark is required
The pair is a diphthong in the first word and a hiatus in the second, which leaves the first stressed on its first syllable and the second on its second
options.misconception: reverses which of the two words keeps the pair together, so the stress is assigned to the wrong word in each case

options.text: The pair is a hiatus in the first word and a diphthong in the second, since a mark always means the pair was split
options.misconception: infers the syllable count from the presence of a mark instead of from the stress on the pair

questions.explanation: The first step of the accent test is counting syllables, and a pair of vowels counts as one syllable unless the stress separates it. A and u normally make one diphthong, so 'causa' is two syllables and the first of them carries the stress; a word stressed on the first of two syllables and ending in a vowel is written with no mark at all, which is what the first word shows. In the second word the u is stressed, and a stressed closed vowel cannot belong to a diphthong, so the two vowels are in hiatus and the word is ba-ul, still two syllables but stressed on the last. A hiatus made of a stressed closed vowel and an open vowel always takes a mark on the closed vowel, whatever the ending of the word happens to be, so 'baúl' is written the way it is even though the ending -l would by itself have required nothing. That last point is the trap in the fourth option and in the usual learner version of this rule: a syllable count of two is not enough to place either word, because the same count can be stressed on the first syllable or on the second, and the two cases are decided by different parts of the test.
questions.hint: Ask whether the stress falls on the u, and what a stressed closed vowel does to a pair.

questions.topic: Endings in n and s, and the position of the stress
questions.learningObjective: apply the rule for endings in n and s to a word that needs no accent
questions.stem: The words 'tambien' and 'despues' are printed in a Spanish text without their accents, while the word 'crisis' is printed correctly with no accent at all. What single rule separates those three cases correctly?

options.text: Every word ending in n or s takes a written accent, whatever its stress
options.misconception: takes the ending on its own as sufficient reason for a written accent

options.text: A word ending in n or s takes the accent exactly when the last syllable is the stressed one
No word ending in n or s takes an accent, since that ending is already audible in speech
options.misconception: believes a final n or s makes the written accent redundant

options.text: The accent depends only on how many syllables the word has, and not on the stress at all
options.misconception: decides the accent from a syllable count and ignores where the stress falls

questions.explanation: Tambien is tam-bien and despues is des-pues: both end in n or s and both are stressed on the last syllable, so both take a written accent. Crisis is cri-sis, which has the same ending and the stress on the first syllable, so the rules leave it unmarked, and gratis works the same way. The two wrong answers in the other options are exact mirror images of each other, one refusing accents on this ending and the other granting them automatically, and both come from treating the ending as the whole decision. The stress is never optional in this rule: it is the part that has to be checked first.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Words ending in a consonant other than n or s
questions.learningObjective: state the accent rule for consonant endings together with its exception
questions.stem: A Spanish packing list reads 'papel', 'reloj', 'ciudad' and 'joven'. All four are correctly written without any accent. Which generalisation about that ending is right, and where does it need qualifying?

options.text: The accent is required in all four, since a consonant ending leaves the stress completely unmarked
options.misconception: claims a consonant ending always leaves the stress in need of marking

options.text: Such a word can never carry an accent, not even when the stress moves further forward
options.misconception: states the consonant-ending rule without the exception for esdrújulas such as facil

options.text: The accent appears only when the stress falls on the last syllable, as in a long final vowel
options.misconception: extends the vowel-ending rule to consonants and so invents accents in papel and reloj

options.text: A consonant ending settles the stress on the last syllable, so no accent unless the stress moves forward as in fácil

questions.explanation: A Spanish word ending in a consonant other than n or s is stressed on that last syllable, and the standard rule then says the orthography has nothing to add: papel, reloj, ciudad and joven are all correct as they stand. The rule does need one qualification, because the antepenult rule is stronger than it looks. Facil, util and publico are all esdrújulas: they also end in a consonant, and they do take a written accent. So the ending settles the usual case and defers to the antepenult rule in the exceptional one, which is why a statement without the qualification is not quite safe.
questions.hint: Test the generalisation on a word like fácil before you accept it.

questions.topic: The final syllable left unstressed
questions.learningObjective: recognise a word that needs no accent because the stress is not on its last syllable
questions.stem: A Spanish reader checks three ordinary words in a short text: 'mesa', 'problema' and 'clase'. None of the three carries a written accent. What do the three have in common that a writer can rely on?

options.text: Each one is stressed on the antepenult, so the accent has been left off by mistake
options.misconception: reads an unmarked word as a spelling mistake in the antepenult position

options.text: Each one ends in a vowel, and a final vowel always removes the need for an accent
options.misconception: generalises from the vowel ending and forgets that problema ends differently

options.text: Each one has three or more syllables, and a long word never needs a written accent
options.misconception: believes the number of syllables decides whether an accent is written

options.text: Each one has the stress on a syllable other than the last, so no accent is required

questions.explanation: The three words are all llanas, which means the stress sits somewhere other than the final syllable, and a llana ending in a vowel, n or s is written plain. Mesa is me-sa, problema is pro-ble-ma and clase is cla-se, so in each case the orthography has no work to do. This is the reason the rule is worth learning as a decision rather than as a list: ask first where the stress is, and only then ask what the ending is. A learner who checks the ending first will add accents that do not belong, and a learner who counts syllables will add accents in the wrong place entirely.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A word stressed on the antepenult always takes an accent
questions.learningObjective: use the antepenult rule on a word whose unaccented form is a different word
questions.stem: In Spanish a noun for a practice session and a verb meaning practices are spelled the same way apart from a written accent. A learner writes 'la practica' for the noun, and the teacher insists on 'la práctica' with the stress marked. Why does the teacher win?

options.text: A word ending in a vowel always takes an accent, and the noun happens to end in a vowel
options.misconception: credits the vowel ending instead of the position of the stress

options.text: A word of three syllables always takes an accent, including words that end in n or s
options.misconception: replaces the antepenult rule with a syllable count and over-applies it

options.text: A word takes an accent only when the stress falls on its first syllable, which is rare
options.misconception: confuses the antepenult position with the first syllable

options.text: A word stressed on the antepenult always takes an accent, whatever ending it happens to have

questions.explanation: Practica as a noun is prac-ti-ca, stressed on the antepenult, and the antepenult rule is absolute: a Spanish word with the stress on the antepenult is always esdrújula and always written with a written accent, whatever its ending. The unaccented practica is a different word, the verb she practises, which is prac-ti-ca with the stress on the last syllable and therefore needs no accent. This pair is a good example of why the rule matters beyond the classroom, because a reader who has never met the rule sees the two spellings as variants of one word and cannot tell which one a text means.
questions.hint: Say the noun aloud and count back from the end: which syllable carries the stress?

questions.topic: The one-syllable words that carry a written accent
questions.learningObjective: apply the weak-vowel rule to one-syllable words
questions.stem: A Spanish spelling test asks about one-syllable words only, and 'un', 'el', 'por', 'con' and 'tu' are among the words that never take a written accent. Which group of one-syllable words does take one?

options.text: Every monosyllable ending in a consonant, such as 'mes', 'ten' and 'dos'
options.misconception: ties the accent to the ending and ignores the vowel inside the word

options.text: Every monosyllable ending in a vowel, such as 'pan', 'mar' and 'fin'
options.misconception: carries the rule for longer words over to a single syllable

options.text: Every monosyllable containing an unstressed e or o, such as 'qué', 'más' and 'tú' the pronoun
No monosyllable at all, since a word of one syllable never needs its stress marked
options.misconception: believes stress marking is unnecessary in a one-syllable word

questions.explanation: In a one-syllable word there is no second syllable for an accent to contrast with, so the accent is not marking stress; it is doing another job. The job it does is keeping two different words apart, and it is needed exactly when the word contains an unstressed e or o: the question word beside the conjunction, the quantity adverb beside the conjunction, the pronoun beside the possessive. Mes, ten and dos contain no such vowel and are left unmarked, which is why the first and the last options both go wrong. The command form of dar and the command of saber follow the same rule for the same reason.
questions.hint: Look for the weak vowel e or o inside each one-syllable word.

questions.learningObjective: keep the two words spelled de and de apart in writing
questions.stem: A Spanish speaker asks a colleague to stop arguing and writes 'Dejame hablar'. The colleague objects that the sentence as written breaks a word into a preposition and an impossible verb form. What is the correct spelling, and what makes it necessary?

options.text: 'Dejame', because a written accent is dropped whenever the register is informal
options.misconception: believes formality decides whether a written accent is written

options.text: 'Dejame', because dar is irregular and irregular verbs never take a written accent
options.misconception: ties the accent to the irregularity of the verb rather than to the homograph

options.text: 'Dejame', but only when the speaker means the formal command addressed to one person
options.misconception: believes the accent belongs to the usted command and not to the tuteo command

options.text: 'Déjame', because the command of dar has to be marked apart from the preposition de

Bare de is a preposition used before an infinitive, a noun or a pronoun, and a writer who leaves the accent off produces a sequence that is not a word at all, which is why a reader cannot repair it by guessing. options.text: every word that ends in a vowel, and none of the words that end in a consonant
options.misconception: applies the ending of the word as the sole test and so misses miercoles

options.text: day, days, most, Wednesday, here, coffee, menu and is, which is eight words in all
day, days, most, Wednesday, here, coffee and menu, but not the form of is in the last line
options.misconception: misses the one word that takes the accent as a verb rather than as an adverb

questions.learningObjective: choose between the two words spelled mas in a sentence about quantity
questions.stem: A Spanish speaker says 'No quiero más café, sino té'. A colleague copies the sentence and leaves the first of the two words unmarked. What correction does the written accent require, and what is the reason for it?

options.text: Both words take an accent, because two words of one syllable in a row must be marked
options.misconception: extends the weak-vowel rule to the conjunction, which has a strong vowel

options.text: The second word becomes 'más', because a conjunction joining two nouns takes an accent
options.misconception: marks the conjunction and leaves the quantity adverb unmarked

options.text: Neither needs it, because a one-syllable word can never need a written accent in Spanish

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the singular is stressed on its last syllable, so it is the kind of word whose mark depends on how it ends, and the only endings that oblige a mark there are a vowel, n and s. Every noun in these two families ends in a d, which is none of the three, so the rule positively forbids a mark and not merely leaves it out. Stage two: the plural adds an s and a syllable, and adding a syllable moves the stress off the last syllable and onto the one before it, so the plural is now a different kind of word from the singular. A word stressed on the syllable before the last takes a mark only when it ends in a consonant other than n or s, and the plural ends in an s, so again nothing is written. The two reasons are not substitutes for one another, and that is the practical point: a learner who reuses the singular's reason on the plural will look at the s and expect a mark, and a learner who reuses the plural's reason on the singular will land on the right spelling for the wrong reason and will not be able to handle a word in the family that is long enough to behave differently.

A learner who applies the general rule mechanically will put the mark on the syllable they think carries the stress and produce a spelling no one uses. The single step that resolves both is to look at the ending and the stress in that order, and to ask which of the three classes the word is in before asking anything about the letter: the two numbers of these nouns fall in two different classes, and each class has its own list of endings that oblige a mark. questions.hint: Decide which of the two meanings the sentence needs, then work out where the stress falls.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A plural that moves the stress and gains an accent
questions.learningObjective: predict the accent in a plural whose ending breaks a diphthong
questions.stem: A Spanish speaker writes 'joven' and then 'jóvenes', and later 'ángel' and 'ángeles'. What has the plural ending done in the second pair of words?

options.text: Nothing changes, since a plural always keeps the stress and the mark of its singular
options.misconception: supposes the general pattern about plurals has no exceptions of this kind

options.text: The mark is added to the singular as well, so that the two words match each other
options.misconception: spreads the mark backwards and breaks a pair that is correct as it stands

options.text: The ending begins with a vowel, so the diphthong breaks and the word becomes esdrújula with a mark
The ending begins with a vowel, so the stress moves to the last syllable and the mark is dropped
options.misconception: gets the syllable count right and then moves the stress in the wrong direction

questions.explanation: When a plural ending begins with a vowel, it can break a diphthong that stood in the singular, and the syllable count rises with the stress staying where it was. The word for a young person has two syllables in the singular and three in the plural, with the stress on the first, which is the antepenult, and so the plural is written with a mark. The same happens to a word that ends in a stressed diphthong before the ending. The general pattern about a plural keeping its stress is still true, and this case shows that the pattern and the accent have to be considered together.
questions.hint: Count the syllables of each form and see whether the vowel pair is still one syllable.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The spelling of the s and c sounds in two varieties
questions.learningObjective: compare the established spelling of the s and c sounds in Spain and in Latin America

stimulus.body: Extracto A, de un manual impreso en España: 'La acción se organizó en el aula.' Extracto B, de un manual impreso en Colombia: 'La accion se organizo en el aula.'
stimulus.license: Original text written for this item by the author; no third-party text is reproduced.

questions.stem: The two extracts print the same sentence with a different letter. Which statement about the difference is accurate?

options.text: Both are established forms in their own variety, because the two countries pronounce the sounds differently
Extract B is a misspelling, since the letter c is the only correct one before the vowel i
options.misconception: treats one variety's spelling as the only correct form in the language

options.text: Both are wrong, since the noun and the verb in the sentence should carry no accent at all
options.misconception: denies the accents that both varieties write, and misses the point of the comparison

options.text: The difference is a matter of typing, since the two letters sit on the same key in some keyboards
options.misconception: explains a difference of orthographic norm as a difference of keyboard layout

questions.explanation: Spanish writes one sound in more than one way, and the letters s and c before e and i are one of those cases: in a variety where the two sounds are kept apart, the written form carries the distinction, and in a variety where they are merged, the established form uses the s alone. Both spellings are correct within their own variety, and neither is an error, which is why a reader who knows only one of them should not correct the other. The accents in the sentence are a separate matter and are written in both, so the third option fails on a point that the comparison does not turn on.
questions.hint: Ask whether the two varieties keep the two sounds apart, and what follows for the spelling.

questions.topic: Three short words written with the letters h and ll
questions.learningObjective: keep three short words of the same shape apart by their letters
questions.stem: Three short Spanish words share almost the same letters: 'halla', 'haya' and 'aya'. A writer needs the command that means look, the kind of wood, and the person who minds a child. Which pairing is right?

options.text: The command keeps the two l's of its verb, the wood takes a y in the place of the second l, and the nursemaid is written with no h at all
The command takes an h and a y, since it belongs to the same verb as the wood
options.misconception: makes two different words of two different verbs identical, and so loses the contrast entirely

options.text: The wood takes the two l's, since the tree and the search are spelled alike in writing
options.misconception: gives the word for the tree the spelling of the command and swaps the two functions

options.text: The command takes the two l's, the wood takes a y, and the nursemaid takes an h in front of the vowel
options.misconception: reinstates a silent h in front of a vowel, which is the rule the three words exist to disprove

questions.explanation: The command is written with two l's because it belongs to the verb whose forms keep that cluster, and the imperative is a fixed form that never drops them. The word for a beech is written with a y, and it belongs to a different verb altogether, which is why the two cannot be brought under one spelling. The word for a nursemaid is written with a plain a and no h: the h in front of a vowel is normally silent, and that is why the same verb appears elsewhere as haber and here with the letter dropped. Three words of five letters, three different functions, and no way to spell them by ear, which is the practical point of the set. The rejected options each merge two of the three or restore the silent h, and both of those moves produce a form no one writes.
questions.hint: Decide which of the three belongs to which verb before you look at the letters.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Where the letter x is written and where it is not
questions.learningObjective: place the letter x in a name and leave it out of the derived adjectives
questions.stem: A Spanish textbook names two countries and gives a word for a person or a thing from each. Which pair is written correctly?

options.text: 'México' and 'mexicano', because the letter belongs to the name and is not carried over into the common word built from it
'México' and 'méxicano', because a name should be respelled by the ordinary rules in the common word built from it
options.misconception: respells a proper name in a derived word, so the name and the common noun end up with the same letters for no reason

options.text: 'Kazajistán' and 'kazajo', because the letters k and s of a name are always replaced in the word derived from it
options.misconception: states two words that really are written that way and gives a rule that does not produce them

options.text: 'México' and 'mexicane', because the ending of the derived word is chosen from the last letter of the name
options.misconception: invents an ending rule from the final letter of a proper name, which fixes nothing

questions.explanation: The x in a country name is a fact about that name and not a general rule about the language, so it stays in the name and does not travel into the common word: 'México' keeps it and 'mexicano' has no x at all. The same shape appears in the other pair, where the name keeps a k and an s and the derived word has neither, so the version about the pair with a k and an s names two words that really are written that way while giving a rule that could not produce them, which is the sharpest trap in the item: the pair is right and the reason is invented. The general shape is that a proper name may keep a letter for historical reasons, while the common words built from it are spelled like any other word, and a learner who carries the letter across will write a form no one uses. The other rejected option invents an ending from the last letter of the name, which fixes nothing and is not a pattern any other language shares either.
questions.hint: Ask whether the letter belongs to the name or to the ordinary spelling of a common word.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The demonstratives in older texts and under the 2010 rules
questions.learningObjective: state how the demonstratives are written under the 2010 rules and what they were like before
questions.stem: Explain to a learner how the Spanish demonstratives are written in ordinary modern use, and say what a reader of an older book will find in them.

answer.exemplar: In ordinary modern Spanish the demonstratives are written without an accent: este, ese, aquel and the neuter esto, eso and aquello, whether they are used as adjectives or as pronouns. Before the 2010 rules they were commonly written with a tilde when they stood alone as pronouns, and a text printed before that date will show a form that looks accented. The change followed the same principle as the change to the adverb solo, which is that one syllable does not need its stress marked, and the two changes together are why a reader of an old book may find two sets of spellings for the same words. A learner should know both sets, not only the new one, because a mark that older books use is not a mistake in them, and treating it as one makes an old text unreadable.

questions.explanation: This item fails in one characteristic way, which is that a learner who knows only the new spelling reads the old one as an error rather than as a date. That is why the second half of the question matters: the older forms were correct when they were printed, and a reader has to recognise them to understand what a text from the twentieth century is saying. The underlying principle is the one the 2010 rules applied, that a mark is written to do a job and a job that no longer exists does not need one, which also explains the change in the adverb that means only. Stating the principle lets a learner place a new spelling it has not met before.
questions.hint: Ask what the 2010 rules decided about a single syllable, and check it against the adverb that means only.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: The conjunction o and the question words that take an accent
questions.learningObjective: mark the question words of an interrogative series and leave the conjunction o plain
questions.stem: A Spanish speaker asks a question with three alternatives: 'Dónde, cuándo y dónde voy a comer?' A learner says the third word needs the accent as well. What is the position?

options.text: None of the three takes the accent, since a series of alternatives is not a question
options.misconception: denies the interrogative force of the series and loses the rule for all of them

options.text: The conjunction takes the accent and the question words do not, since a question is a statement
options.misconception: inverts the two and misdescribes the function of the whole phrase

options.text: The question words in the series take the accent, and the conjunction o between them never does
All three words take the accent, since they are all alternatives in the same question
options.misconception: gives the conjunction a mark because it stands among accented words

questions.explanation: The interrogative words take a mark when they are being used as such, and in a series of alternatives they keep it: donde, cuando, quien, cual, como and the phrase por que are written with one. The conjunction o is different, because its o is a strong vowel that never takes a mark, and a learner who sees a series of marked words will often mark the o as well. The result is a question that looks regular and is not, which is why the rule is worth stating as two halves: mark the question words, and leave the conjunction alone whatever else in the sentence carries a mark.
questions.hint: Decide, of each of the three words, whether it is asking something or joining two alternatives.

questions.topic: The written contractions a el and de el
questions.learningObjective: apply the two written contractions and say where they do not apply
questions.stem: A Spanish writer has to choose between four ways of writing two phrases: 'voy a el hospital' or 'voy al hospital', and 'vengo de el trabajo' or 'vengo del trabajo'. Which pair does the written language use?

options.text: Both contracted, since a and de are written joined to the masculine article in the singular
Neither contracted, since a contraction is spoken and never written in Spanish
options.misconception: believes a written contraction does not exist and rejects the standard form

options.text: Both contracted, including before a pronoun, as in a el and de el for that person
options.misconception: over-applies the contraction and breaks the phrases with a pronoun

options.text: Only the first contracted, since the preposition de never joins the article in writing
options.misconception: halves the rule and leaves one of the two standard forms out

questions.explanation: Two of the prepositions join with the masculine article in the singular in writing as well as in speech: a el becomes al and de el becomes del. Nothing else joins, so a la, a los, de la and de los stay apart, and the phrase with the pronoun that names a person keeps its preposition separate, which is why that case is the exception the third option describes. The same distinction shows up in a word the learner already knows, since a language that has al and del as single written words does not also have a separate form of them.
questions.hint: Ask which two prepositions can join with the article, and what makes that pair different.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: A whole accent test applied to one list of words
questions.learningObjective: apply the full accent test to a list and justify each decision
questions.stem: A Spanish teacher gives a class a list of six ordinary words and asks each student to say, for every one of them, whether it takes a written accent and why. Explain the order of the test and how it settles a word whose stress is not obvious from the spelling.

answer.exemplar: The test has three questions and they come in this order. First, how many syllables has the word, counting a diphthong as one, because the answer tells the learner which of three classes the word belongs to. Second, which syllable is stressed, because that is what every rule then operates on. Third, what does the word end in, since the ending decides the mark in all but the antepenult class. Applying it: a word stressed on its antepenult always takes a mark whatever its ending, a word stressed on its last syllable takes one when it ends in a vowel, in n or in s, and a word stressed on the syllable before the last takes one only when it ends in a consonant other than n or s. When the spelling does not make the stress obvious, which is what happens with a two-syllable word ending in a vowel or in n or s, the test cannot answer and the learner has to say the word aloud, find the stress that way, and then apply the rule. Saying that honestly is part of the answer, because a method that pretends the spelling settles everything will be wrong on exactly those words.

questions.explanation: The question asks for an order and a method, so an answer that lists six answers without a method does not meet it, and an answer that gives the order without saying what to do when the spelling runs out also falls short. The pair of failures is worth naming: a learner who asks about the ending first produces accents in the wrong place, and a learner who believes the spelling always settles the stress will misjudge every two-syllable word ending in a vowel, n or s, which is a large part of the vocabulary. A good answer therefore ends by admitting the limit of the method, since the honest instruction for those words is to say them aloud.
questions.hint: Ask which question has to come first, and which words the third question cannot settle.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Correcting a short notice and naming the rule behind each correction
questions.learningObjective: correct every accent in a short text and name the rule that governs each one

stimulus.body: REUNION: El sabado, a las nueve, el monitor trae el material. La sala esta ocupada, y el curso se traslada a la biblioteca. El guardian entrega las llaves del almacen pequeno el dia siguiente.
stimulus.license: Original notice written for this item by the author; no third-party text is reproduced.

questions.stem: Stage one: list every word in the notice that needs a written accent. Stage two: for each correction, name the part of the accent test that requires it.

answer.exemplar: Stage one, the eight words that need a written accent, in the four groups the accent test produces. REUNION, sabado, almacen and pequeno are all esdrújulas: three syllables with the stress on the first, and for that class the test stops at the syllable count, because the class always takes a mark whatever the ending is. pequeno needs two marks rather than one and this is worth saying out loud, because the squiggle on the n is a letter and the accent on the e is the one the rule asks for; a learner who treats the two as one mark either writes pequeno and loses the letter or leaves both off. monitor is the one that looks easiest and is not: mo-ni-tor, three syllables with the stress in the middle, a llana, and a llana that ends in a consonant other than n or s takes a mark, so the i carries it. esta is the only correction that needs a step before the accent test, because the same six letters spell a demonstrative, esta mesa, which carries no mark, so the decision comes from the function and not from the letters. guardian is the trap in the other direction: a learner who has learned that words ending in n take nothing will leave it alone, but that rule covers a word whose stress falls on the penult, whereas guardian is guar-dian, two syllables with the stress on the second, an aguda ending in n, and an aguda that ends in n takes a mark. dia is the second trap, and the more interesting one, because the ending rule on its own would say no: the stress is on the first of two syllables and the word ends in a vowel, which is the shape that takes nothing. What settles it is the shape of the stressed syllable. The i there is a closed vowel and it is followed by the open a, so the two vowels are not a diphthong but a hiatus, and a hiatus between a stressed closed vowel and an open vowel takes a mark whatever the ending of the word happens to be. Stage two, the deciding question for each entry, always in this order: count the syllables, say which syllable is stressed, look at the ending, and only then ask whether two vowels are in contact. The words left alone are what separates a real answer from a lucky one. sala, curso, biblioteca and the two uses of dia that belong to a noun rather than a numeral are all llanas ending in a vowel, so nothing goes on them. el is left alone for the ordinary reason, since the article is unstressed and the pronoun that carries a mark is not in the notice. Naming the deciding question for each entry is what makes the list reusable on a notice the learner has not seen.

questions.explanation: The two stages separate two skills that are usually mixed together, and the separation is what makes the item work. A learner can find the words that need a mark and still be unable to say why, and the reason is the part that transfers to a new text. The two characteristic errors in the notice are instructive: the verb beside its demonstrative homograph, which is decided by the function rather than by the letters, and the noun whose unstressed ending makes it look as if the stress were further forward than it is. A response that lists corrections without the reasoning will have got the notice right and will fail on the next one.
questions.hint: Do the list first, then go back through it and name the deciding question for each entry.

questions.subject: SPANISH
questions.topic: Deciding the article for an unfamiliar noun in two stages
questions.learningObjective: work out the gender of a new noun from its ending and from what it is used for
questions.stem: Stage one: say what a Spanish speaker can conclude about the gender of a noun from its ending alone, and name the two families where the ending is decisive. Stage two: say what the speaker should do when the noun ends in o or in a consonant and no rule applies.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: a noun ending in -a is feminine and a noun ending in -o is masculine, with the two small families of exceptions on each side, which is the rule that settles most of the vocabulary. The two families where the ending is decisive in the other direction are the nouns of Greek origin in -ma, which are masculine although they end in a vowel a, and the everyday nouns la mano, la moto and la foto, which are feminine although they end in o. Stage two: with a noun ending in o or in a consonant, and no memory of the word, the speaker cannot conclude anything from the ending and has to find the gender some other way, and the reliable ways are to look the word up, to hear it from a speaker or to look for an article or an adjective in a text that contains it. A speaker who is about to write the word for the first time can also choose a form that does not commit, which is why the advice to a learner is to look it up rather than to guess, since a guessed gender is corrected in every sentence in which it is wrong.

questions.explanation: The two stages test different things and a response that only does the first will sound confident and be wrong. Stage one is the rule, and every speaker applies it constantly, usually without noticing. Stage two is the harder and more useful half, because it asks what to do when the rule has nothing to say, and the honest answer is that the ending has to be set aside and the word has to be found in a dictionary, in a text, or in the mouth of a speaker. The failure this item is built around is the learner who treats the masculine as a default for any word they do not recognise, which produces a wrong article in every sentence until the word is looked up.
questions.hint: Ask what the ending can prove, and what a speaker does when it cannot prove anything.
